questions.question: For `x <- c(-2, 3)`, the call `ifelse(x > 0, x, 0)` returns `[1] 0 3`, while `if (x > 0) x else 0` stops with an error. What explains the difference?
options: `ifelse()` looks only at the first element of `x > 0`, so its test is one value
`if` cannot return a vector such as `x`, only a single number
`ifelse()` decides each position separately; `if` needs one `TRUE` or `FALSE`
`if` needs one `else if` block per element of `x`, and here they are missing

questions.question: For a numeric vector `x` with elements $x_i$, what does `ifelse(x > 0, 1, 0)` compute in position $i$?
options: the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\{x\colon x>0\}}(x_i)$
the positive part $\max(x_i, 0)$ of $x_i$
the sign of $x_i$, equal to $-1$, $0$ or $1$
the count of positive values among $x_1,\dots,x_i$

questions.question: What does R return for `x <- c(-3, 2, 0); ifelse(x > 0, x^2, -x)`?
What does R return for `ifelse(c(2, NA, 7) > 5, "high", "low")`?
options: `[1] "low"  "low"  "high"`
`[1] "low"  NA     "high"`
`[1] "low"  "high"`
the error `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed`

questions.question: Which labels does `x <- c(-3, 0, 4); ifelse(x < 0, "-", ifelse(x == 0, "0", "+"))` produce?
options: an error, as the inner call returns three values for single positions

questions.question: What does R return for `x <- c(2, -1, 5, 0); sum(ifelse(x > 0, 1, 0))`?
Which line changes a numeric vector `x` without missing values in the same way as `x[x < 0] <- 0`?
options: `ifelse(x < 0, 0, x)`
`x <- ifelse(x < 0, x, 0)`
`x <- ifelse(x < 0, 0)`
`x <- ifelse(x < 0, 0, x)`

questions.question: What does R return for `day <- c("Mon", "Sat", "Sun"); ifelse(day %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "weekend", "weekday")`?
options: `[1] "weekday" "weekend"`
`[1] "weekend"`
`[1] "weekday" "weekend" "weekend"`
`[1] "weekday" "weekday" "weekday"`

questions.question: What does R return for `x <- c(5, -2); ifelse(x > 0, x, "neg")`?
options: a character vector, printed as `[1] "5"   "neg"`
a vector holding the number 5 and the text `"neg"`, each with its own type
the numeric vector `[1]  5 NA`, as text cannot be stored with numbers
an error, as `yes` and `no` have different types

questions.question: For `x <- c(4, -1, 7)`, how do `ifelse(x > 0, x, NA)` and the logical subset `x[x > 0]` differ?
options: They are identical: both return the positive values `4 7`.
`ifelse()` returns `4 7`, while `x[x > 0]` returns `4 NA 7`.
Both keep three positions, but `x[x > 0]` puts 0 where the test fails.
`ifelse()` keeps all three positions, `4 NA 7`; `x[x > 0]` keeps only `4 7`.

questions.question: To label each element of `x <- c(5, 15, -1)` as `"in"` when it lies strictly between 0 and 10, why must the test be `x > 0 & x < 10` rather than `x > 0 && x < 10`?
options: `&&` works only on numbers, while `&` also accepts logical values
`&` combines element by element; `&&` takes single values and stops for length 3
Both give the same test, but `&` is faster on long vectors
`&&` asks whether all elements are in range, so every label becomes `"out"`

questions.question: What does R return for `ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE), c(1, 2), c(10, 20))`?
options: an error, as `yes` and `no` are shorter than the test

questions.question: What does R return for `p <- c(5, 12, 25); ifelse(p > 10, "mid", ifelse(p > 20, "high", "low"))`?
options: `[1] "low" "mid" "mid"`
`[1] "low"  "mid"  "high"`
`[1] "low"  "low"  "high"`
an error, as `p > 10` and `p > 20` overlap

questions.question: For a numeric vector `x` without missing values, which code gives the same result as `ifelse(x > 0, 1, -1)` for every such `x`?
options: `y <- if (x > 0) 1 else -1`
`y <- rep(0, length(x)); for (i in seq_along(x)) { y <- if (x[i] > 0) 1 else -1 }`
`y <- rep(0, length(x)); for (i in seq_along(x)) { y[i] <- if (x[i] > 0) 1 else -1 }`

questions.question: Which vector does `ifelse(x > 0, cumsum(x), 0)` produce for `x <- c(2, -1, 3)`?
Meaning "if `n` is positive use the vector `c(1, 2, 3)`, otherwise 0", a student writes `ifelse(n > 0, c(1, 2, 3), 0)` with `n <- 5` and gets `[1] 1`. Why?
options: `ifelse()` always returns a single value, just like `if`
`yes` is cut to the length of `no`, the single number 0
The result has the length of the test, 1, so only `yes[1]` is used
R warns that `c(1, 2, 3)` is too long and then keeps its first value

questions.question: For numeric vectors `a` and `b` of the same length without missing values, which statement compares `ifelse(a > b, a, b)` with `ifelse(a >= b, a, b)` correctly?
options: They always agree: where `a[i]` equals `b[i]`, both pick the same number.
They differ wherever `a[i]` equals `b[i]`, as one takes `b[i]` and the other `a[i]`.
The first gives the element-wise maximum, the second the element-wise minimum.
Both return one number, the largest value found in `a` and `b` together.

questions.question: The call `ifelse(x > 0, x, ifelse(is.na(x), 0, -x))` is meant to give the absolute value, with 0 for missing values. What does it give for `x <- c(-2, NA, 3)`?
options: the error `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed`
`[1] NA NA NA`

questions.question: To keep the positive values of `x <- c(-1, 4, -2, 9)` and put 0 elsewhere, a student writes `ifelse(x > 0, x[x > 0], 0)`. What does R return?
options: an error, as `x[x > 0]` is shorter than the test
